Brazilian officials first raised concerns with Apple nearly three months ago about minors' ability to access gambling apps, and the iPhone maker has now been given five business days to provide further information on the safety measures in its App Store. Here's what we know so far.

Apple faces regulatory and age verification pressure

Back in April, Brazilian officials wrote separately to Apple and Google, questioning the lack of age restrictions on gambling apps in their app stores.

At the time, the National Secretariat for Digital Rights (Sedigi) and the National Consumer Secretariat (Senacon) each sent letters to the two companies, asking whether there were "a significant number" of apps on their platforms that offered or facilitated minors' access to gambling platforms.

Brazil recently passed new legislation known as "ECA Digital," requiring app stores to restrict minors' access to gambling content — Apple subsequently rolled out age verification features in the country for apps rated 18+.

However, officials said their preliminary investigation found that many gambling apps appeared to lack proper age restrictions or federal authorisation, raising questions about the effectiveness of the safeguards in place.

While Apple's full response has not been made public, authorities now say the company has answered most of the initial questions, but more information is still needed.

Below is a statement issued by Brazil's Ministry of Justice and Public Security (published via Canaltech):

Items still to be clarified include: how to verify the regulatory authorisation of apps offered in Brazil; the technical criteria used to distinguish simulation-type apps from those involving real-money gambling — including cases where approved features are subsequently hidden or altered; and existing mechanisms to prevent minors from accessing inappropriate content. Authorities also requested information on proactive monitoring procedures, risk prioritisation criteria, the average takedown time after detection, and the implementation and publication schedule of remedial measures (including

The secretariat said Google's response was weaker and has asked the search giant to further explain: how it verifies the identity of authorised operators, how it monitors apps whose licences have been suspended or expired, how it measures enforcement effectiveness, and how it prevents minors from searching for or downloading gambling apps.

Finally, the secretariat demanded that responses from both Apple and Google be made public, but allowed confidential material to be submitted separately under restricted arrangements.
